# Box Plots {#box}

## Introduction

In this chapter, we will learn to

- create univariate/multivariate box plots
- interpret box plots
- create horizontal box plots
- detect outliers
- modify box color
- use formula to compare distributions of different variables
- use notches to compare medians

## Box Plot

A box plot is a standardized way of displaying the distribution of data based on the five-number summary: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum. Box plots are useful for detecting outliers and for comparing distributions, and they show the shape, central tendency and variability of the data.

### Structure

A box plot splits the data set into quartiles. The body of the box plot consists of a "box" (hence the name), which goes from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3). Within the box, a vertical line is drawn at Q2, the median of the data set. Two horizontal lines, called whiskers, extend from the front and back of the box. The front whisker goes from Q1 to the smallest non-outlier in the data set, and the back whisker goes from Q3 to the largest non-outlier. If the data set includes one or more outliers, they are plotted separately as points on the chart. 

## Univariate Box Plot

### Basic Plot

Let us begin by creating a basic box plot. We will use the `boxplot()` function and specify the data.

```{r box1, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)
```

### Horizontal Box Plot

Use the `horizontal` argument in the `boxplot()` function to create a horizontal box plot.

```{r box2, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg, horizontal = TRUE)
```

### Color

Let us add some color to the box plot. Use the `col` argument to specify a color for the plot.

```{r box3, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg, col = 'blue')
```

### Border Color

We can specify a separate color for the border of the box. To modify the border color, use the `border` argument.

```{r box4, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg, border = 'red')
```

### Range

The `range` argument determines how far the plot whiskers extend out from the box. If range is positive, the whiskers extend to the most extreme data point that is no more than range times the interquartile range from the box. A value of zero makes the whiskers extend to the data extremes.

Let us set the value of `range` to 0 and observe the plot.

```{r box5, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg, range = 0)
```

In the below plot, we set the value of `range` to 1.

```{r box6, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg, range = 1)
```

Let us observe how the plot appears as we change the value of `range` from 0 to 1.

```{r box7, fig.align='center', fig.width=10, fig.height=10, echo=FALSE}
init <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
values <- c(0, 0.25, 0.63, 1)
for (i in values) {
  boxplot(mtcars$mpg, range = i)
  mtext(paste("range = ", i), side = 3, col = "blue")
}
par(init)
```

### Outline

The outliers in the plot are not drawn if the `outline` argument is set to `FALSE`. The default is `TRUE`.

```{r box8, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg, range = 1, outline = FALSE)
```

The below plot displays how the plot changes with the values set for `outline`:

```{r box9, fig.align='center', fig.width=10, fig.height=5, echo=FALSE}
init <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
values <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
for (i in values) {
  boxplot(mtcars$mpg, outline = i, range = 1)
  mtext(paste("outline = ", i), side = 3, col = "blue")
}
par(init)
```

### Varwidth

If the `varwidth` argument is set to `TRUE`, the boxes are drawn with widths proportional to the square root of the number of observations in each group.

```{r, fig.align='center', fig.width=10, fig.height=5, echo=FALSE}
#| label: fig-box-summary
#| fig-cap: "The five-number summary drawn on the same scale as the box plot"
#| fig-alt: "A horizontal strip showing a box plot of a grouped variable alongside text marking the minimum, lower hinge, median, upper hinge and maximum, positioned so each statistic lines up with the corresponding feature of the box."
init <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
values <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
for (i in values) {
  boxplot(mtcars$mpg, varwidth = i, range = 1)
  mtext(paste("varwidth = ", i), side = 3, col = "blue")
}
par(init)
```

## Bivariate/Multivariate Box Plot

As we said in the introduction, box plots can be used to compare distributions of several variables. Let us use the `mtcars` data set and compare the distribution of Miles Per Gallon (`mpg`) for automobiles with different numbers of cylinders (`cyl`), specifying a formula as shown in the example below.

```{r box11, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
```

We use the formula when we compare the distribution of a continuous variable across the levels of a categorical variable. To compare the distributions without a categorical variable, we specify the variables separately in the `boxplot()` function. Below is an illustration of this method: we split the `mpg` data using the `split()` function and plot the parts separately. `split()` splits a continuous variable based on the levels of a categorical variable.

```{r box12, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5, collapse=TRUE}
mpg_split <- split(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl)

mpg_split

mpg_4 <- mpg_split$`4`
mpg_6 <- mpg_split$`6`
mpg_8 <- mpg_split$`8`

boxplot(mpg_4, mpg_6, mpg_8)
```

The same plot can be created in two ways. If you are comparing the distribution of a continuous variable across the levels of a categorical variable, use the formula. If you are comparing the distributions of independent variables, specify all the variables in the `boxplot()` function.

### Color

Let us add some color to the plot. We can specify as many colors as there are boxes, or the same color for all of them. Below are two examples: the same color in the first, different colors in the second.

#### Single Color

```{r box14, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl, col = 'blue')
```

#### Different Colors

```{r box15, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl, 
        col = c('red', 'blue', 'yellow'))
```

### Compare Medians

If we want to test whether the medians of the different groups differ, we can use the `notch` argument and set it to `TRUE`. A notch is drawn in each side of the boxes, and if the notches do not overlap, it is strong evidence that the medians differ.

We will use a different data set for this example. We use the `hsb2` data (High School and Beyond survey, 200 observations; vendored as `data/hsb2.csv`, originally from the UCLA Institute for Digital Research and Education) and compare the distribution of reading score (`read`) for males and females (`female`).

```{r box16, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
hsb <- read.csv('data/hsb2.csv')
boxplot(hsb$read ~ hsb$female, notch = TRUE, 
        col = c('red', 'blue'))
```

Since the notches overlap, there is no strong evidence that the medians differ.

## Putting it all together

Let us conclude by adding a title and axis labels to the box plot. 

```{r box17, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl, range = 1, outline = TRUE, 
        horizontal = TRUE, col = c('red', 'blue', 'yellow'),
        main = 'Miles Per Gallon by Cylinders', 
        ylab = 'Number of Cylinders', xlab = 'Miles Per Gallon',
        names = c('Four', 'Six', 'Eight'))
```
